Abstract
Training large neural networks with data-parallel stochastic gradient descent al-
locates N GPU replicas to compute effectively identical updates—a practice that
leaves the rich space of learning rate configurations entirely unexplored during
training. We propose Hyperparameter-Divergent Ensemble Training (HDET),
a method that repurposes these replicas for simultaneous learning rate exploration
at negligible communication overhead. HDET operates in alternating phases: a
fan-out stage in which replicas train independently under a structured, symmetric
spread of learning rates, and a converge stage in which parameters are averaged
across all replicas via AllReduce every T steps. Building on this ensemble sub-
strate, we further propose an automatic learning rate (auto-LR) controller that
treats the relative training loss across replicas as a performance signal, updating the
shared base schedule toward higher-performing configurations via a momentum-
based gradient-free meta-update. The combined method produces a self-adapting
learning rate schedule that improves both optimization quality and generalization
without additional hyperparameter sweeps or training budget.
Crucially, the framework generalizes beyond learning rate: any scalar hyperparam-
eter that does not alter model architecture—such as dropout rate, attention scale
temperature, or weight-decay coefficient—can be explored across replicas using
the same fan-out/converge protocol, with inter-replica loss differences serving
as zero-order hypergradients that guide the search direction. HDET is imple-
mented as a drop-in replacement for PyTorch’s OneCycleLR scheduler, requiring
no changes to model architecture, optimizer, or data pipeline. Code is available at
https://github.com/hailingc/ensemble_training.
1
Introduction
The learning rate schedule is among the most consequential hyperparameter choices in large-model
training. Popular schedules—one-cycle annealing [Smith and Topin, 2019], cosine decay [Loshchilov
and Hutter, 2017], and linear warmup-decay [Vaswani et al., 2017]—must be specified before training
begins, leaving practitioners to rely on expensive grid searches or heuristics calibrated on smaller
proxy models. Even when a good schedule is found, it may not remain optimal as model or dataset
scale changes across training runs.

Simultaneously, large-model training routinely parallelizes across hundreds of GPU replicas using
data-parallel stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD). In the standard paradigm, every replica maintains
an identical copy of the model parameters and advances under an identical learning rate; the replica’s
sole distinguishing role is the mini-batch it processes. Beyond improving gradient estimates through a
larger effective batch, the additional hardware contributes no qualitative diversity to the optimization
trajectory.
We observe that this uniformity is a missed opportunity. The N parallel replicas could explore
N distinct learning rate trajectories simultaneously, at no additional hardware cost. Moreover, if
those diverging trajectories periodically merge through parameter averaging, the resulting model can
harvest ensemble-like generalization benefits within a single training run.
We formalize this intuition in Hyperparameter-Divergent Ensemble Training (HDET), which
interleaves two phases atop any existing DDP+OneCycleLR setup:
1. Fan-out: each of N GPU replicas trains under a distinct learning rate drawn from a
symmetric spread [¯η (1−α), ¯η (1 +α)] around the current base schedule ¯η(t), where α ≥0
is the spread ratio;
2. Converge: every T training steps, parameters are averaged across all replicas via AllReduce,
producing a unified model that seeds the next fan-out round.
On top of this ensemble substrate we introduce an auto-LR controller that uses the relative training
loss across replicas as a performance signal. Replicas with below-average loss receive proportionally
higher weight in a softmax-weighted average of per-rank learning rates; the resulting performance
deviation drives a momentum-based velocity that shifts the base schedule up or down at each sync
point. If high-LR replicas consistently outperform low-LR ones, the base schedule adapts upward; if
the opposite holds, it adapts downward. This constitutes a gradient-free, within-run optimizer over
the learning rate schedule, eliminating the need for a priori schedule selection.
Contributions.
• We propose HDET, a training method that transforms existing DDP replicas into a structured
learning rate exploration ensemble at zero hardware overhead (§3).
• We introduce an automatic LR controller that uses rank-wise loss signals to adaptively
update the learning rate via a gradient-free momentum update, requiring no additional
tuning (§3.4).
• We identify a practical two-stage strategy—warm noisy initialization from a pre-trained
checkpoint followed by HDET ensemble training—that jointly maximizes model quality
and training stability: warm initialization seeds each replica near a high-quality solution,
while periodic weight averaging prevents divergence under aggressive learning rates that
would destabilize either technique alone (§3.5, §4).
• We demonstrate empirically that HDET consistently improves final model quality and
convergence speed on production-scale training tasks (§4).
• We release a reference implementation as a drop-in PyTorch scheduler at https://github.
com/hailingc/ensemble_training.

Related Work
Learning-rate scheduling and online adaptation.
Standard schedules—one-cycle [Smith and
Topin, 2019], cyclical [Smith, 2017], cosine annealing [Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017], and warmup-
decay [Vaswani et al., 2017]—must be fixed before training; OneCycleLR [Paszke et al., 2019]
is the base scheduler HDET subclasses. Online methods eliminate this: Hypergradient Descent
[Baydin et al., 2018], L4 [Rolinek and Martius, 2018], D-Adaptation [Defazio and Mishchenko,
2023], DoG [Ivgi et al., 2023], and Schedule-Free [Defazio et al., 2024] all derive step sizes from
gradient statistics or loss dynamics. HDET differs: its adaptation signal is cross-replica performance
rather than gradient information.
2


Learning-rate diversity and population-style exploration.
Alrao [Blier et al., 2019] assigns
different learning rates within a single network, covering a wide LR range at negligible cost. PBT
[Jaderberg et al., 2017] maintains a population of models, periodically evaluating and copying
hyperparameters from better to worse members. HDET shares concurrent hyperparameter exploration
but reuses existing DDP replicas and merges them by AllReduce averaging rather than replacement,
requiring no extra workers and preserving gradient information from every replica.
Distributed data-parallel training.
Standard DP-SGD [Li et al., 2020] synchronizes gradients via
AllReduce, keeping all ranks at identical parameters θ(t)

Weight averaging and ensemble merging.
SWA [Izmailov et al., 2018], EMA [Ho et al., 2020],
and Model Soups [Wortsman et al., 2022] average model weights sequentially or after training to
reach flatter minima or improve generalization. SWAP [Gupta et al., 2020] extends SWA to parallel
workers trained simultaneously, the setting most similar to HDET; however, SWAP workers share
identical hyperparameters and differ only in effective batch size, whereas HDET deliberately assigns
distinct learning rates across replicas to explore the hyperparameter space before each averaging step.
Worker divergence and periodic synchronization.
EASGD [Zhang et al., 2015], Local SGD
[Haddadpour et al., 2019], DiLoCo [Douillard et al., 2023], and GRAWA [Dimlioglu and Choro-
manska, 2024] all allow workers to drift from a shared solution between sync events to reduce
communication or improve convergence. HDET differs: divergence is intentionally induced by a
structured LR spread while standard synchronized-gradient DDP is retained throughout.
Gradient-free population optimization.
NES [Wierstra et al., 2014] and ES [Salimans et al.,
2017] optimize model parameters via a population of candidates and scalar fitness signals, requiring
no gradient information. HDET’s auto-LR controller borrows this population-signal idea narrowly:
inter-replica losses steer a single shared scalar (the base LR) while standard gradient-based weight
updates remain intact.
Deep ensembles.
Deep Ensembles [Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017] capture epistemic uncertainty
by training N independent models from different initializations, at N× cost; diversity arises primarily
from models reaching different loss basins [Fort et al., 2019]. HDET generates comparable diversity
within a single run by using the LR spread to push replicas toward different basins before averaging.

This is critical when exploring multiple hyperparameters simultaneously (e.g. per-group LRs). Fixed
rank-to-value assignments would create spurious cross-parameter correlations that confound the

each sync. In this paper we demonstrate simultaneous exploration across four optimizer parameter
groups (embedding, no_decay, non_embedding, transformer), whose emergent differential
decay rates are analyzed in §5.

where ¯θ0 is the pre-trained checkpoint, d is the total number of parameters, and ν controls the

Warm initialization alone is insufficient to stabilize training at aggressive learning rates: without
periodic weight averaging, noisy weights compound with high-LR updates and eventually diverge
(the Warm-Init ablation in §4 confirms this). Its role is to supply better-quality starting points for
the ensemble, not to replace the stabilization provided by the fan-out/converge cycle. When HDET
weight averaging is active, warm-init and the auto-LR controller each contribute independently, as
the ablation results demonstrate.

4
Experiments
4.1
Experimental Setup
Task and data.
We evaluate on a production-scale news-feed dataset from a major social network,
comprising one year of user–item interaction logs. Models are trained jointly on three engagement
tasks (Contribution, Like, LongDwell) for one epoch—standard in production settings where the
data stream is non-repeating and any change in training loss directly reflects optimization quality.
Backbone.
All experiments share the same fixed AttnMVP backbone [Cheng, 2026] with identical
architecture, optimizer (Adam), and feature set. Backbone details are orthogonal to HDET and are
reported in Cheng [2026]; our focus is solely on the training dynamics.
HDET configuration.
All variants run on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs (N=8); each single-epoch
run takes ≈30 hours, constraining ablation breadth. Spread α=1/9, giving multipliers spanning
[0.0008, 0.001] with mean 0.0009 (matching the baseline). T=1,000 steps; Swarm=100,000 steps;
auto-LR: β=0.9, σ=0.1, λ=0.5 (fixed, not tuned).
Ablation configurations.
We compare six configurations that isolate each HDET component:
1. Baseline-Low (η=0.0001, no spread): conservative-LR reference.
2. Baseline-High (η=0.0009, no spread): high-LR without ensemble stabilization.
3. Warm-Init (η=0.0009, no spread): warm noisy initialization from a pre-trained checkpoint
(§3.5), no weight averaging. Tests whether initialization alone is sufficient for high-LR
stability.
4. HDET w/o auto-LR (η=0.0009, spread + warm init): fan-out/converge with LR spread
and weight averaging; auto-LR disabled.
5. HDET w/o warm init (η=0.0009, spread + auto-LR): full HDET from a cold start; ablates
warm initialization.
6. HDET (full) (η=0.0009, spread + warm init + auto-LR): complete method.
We report average training loss across the three tasks (lower is better); † denotes training crash.

4.2
Main Results
4.3
Analysis
Stability (Figure 2).
Both Baseline-High and Warm-Init diverge at η=0.0009; HDET trains stably
throughout. Warm-Init diverges more severely than Baseline-High (4.674 vs. 4.169), confirming that
weight averaging—not initialization—is the primary stabilizer.
Quality and ablation.
HDET w/o auto-LR (3.280) already beats Baseline-Low (3.294) at 9×
higher LR, showing that LR spread + weight averaging alone discovers better optima. The two
ablations—w/o auto-LR (3.280) and w/o warm init (3.281)—each contribute independently and
comparably (≈0.013–0.014 each), and HDET (full, 3.277) combines both for the best result. The
auto-LR gain is modest here because the initial schedule is already near-optimal; larger gains are
expected when the hand-tuned baseline is farther from optimal.
7


Statistical reliability.
We repeated training over 10+ independent models; HDET consistently
outperformed Baseline-Low on offline AUC and NE across all replications. The model is deployed in
the production ranking system.
Per-group LR schedules (Figure 3).
Figure 3 shows GPU 0 (peak LR 0.0008 = ρ0 · 0.0009, the
lowest-LR replica) for clarity; the 8-replica mean equals the 0.0009 baseline. The auto-LR controller
produces periodic fluctuations at each sync and drives all groups to a residual LR of ≈0.0002 rather
than near-zero, reflecting its discovery that a non-trivial final LR benefits this task.
5
Discussion
Exploration-exploitation in hyperparameter space.
HDET implements a principled exploration-
exploitation trade-off directly in hyperparameter space. The fan-out phase is the exploration step:
replicas diverge under a structured spread of learning rates, simultaneously probing distinct regions
of the loss landscape that no single schedule could visit concurrently. The converge phase is the
exploitation step: AllReduce averaging collapses the ensemble into a single model that harvests
the best of all explored trajectories, re-anchoring parameters near the consensus of the full replica
population. Because the LR spread always keeps some replicas conservative, this consensus is
guaranteed to lie in a stable region—which is why periodic averaging prevents divergence where a
single aggressive LR cannot. Warm-Init without HDET illustrates the same mechanism in reverse:
with no converge phase to re-anchor parameters, high-LR updates on perturbed weights compound
unchecked until irrecoverable divergence at ∼185K steps.
Emergent differential LR decay.
The auto-LR controller discovers distinct per-group decay rates
without manual specification (Figure 3): transformer decays fastest (dense high-variance gradients
converge quickly), non_decay parameters slowest (flat landscapes absorb gradient signal throughout),
with embeddings and non-embedding layers in between. This ordering mirrors discriminative fine-
tuning [Howard and Ruder, 2018] but emerges automatically from cross-replica loss signals.
Limitations.
HDET’s auto-LR adapts per-group schedules from model performance across repli-
cas, complementing Adam’s [Kingma and Ba, 2014] per-parameter gradient-moment adaptation;
combining them is a natural next step. The three additional hyperparameters (α, T, σ) were fixed
without tuning and consistently outperformed the baseline, though their interaction and architecture-
dependence warrant further study.
6
Conclusion and Future Work
HDET converts the wasted uniformity of DDP replicas into a structured LR exploration ensemble
via a fan-out/converge cycle (O(1/T) extra communication), with an auto-LR controller that adapts
the base schedule online from cross-replica loss signals and warm noisy initialization that seeds
training near a high-quality checkpoint. On a production recommendation model, HDET trains stably
with much higer LR than the LR that causes divergence in standard DDP and achieves a lower final
loss (3.277 vs. 3.294), while its auto-LR controller autonomously discovers the empirically correct
per-group decay ordering (transformer fastest, non-decay slowest).
Future directions.
(i) General hyperparameter exploration. As formalized in Remark 1, any
scalar hyperparameter that does not change model architecture (dropout, weight decay, temperature)
can be substituted for LR, turning the cluster into a zero-cost hyperparameter search engine using
inter-replica losses as hypergradients. (ii) Group-aware initialization. The emergent decay ordering
provides an empirical prior for initializing per-group spread ratios, potentially accelerating group-wise
schedule discovery. (iii) LLM pretraining. Extending HDET to multi-epoch pretraining over hundreds
of billions of tokens offers more sync intervals for the auto-LR to adapt, with warm-init generalized
to early-stage cold starts. (iv) Convergence theory. A formal analysis characterizing the interplay of
LR spread, sync interval, and averaging on convergence and implicit regularization remains an open
question.

Abstract: Training large neural networks with data-parallel stochastic gradient descent al- locates N GPU replicas to compute effectively identical updates—a practice that leaves the rich space of learning rate configurations entirely unexplored during training. We propose Hyperparameter-Divergent Ensemble Training (HDET), a method that repurposes these replicas for simultaneous learning rate exploration at negligible communication overhead. HDET operates in alternating phases: a fan-out stage in which replicas train independently under a structured, symmetric spread of learning rates, and a converge stage in which parameters are averaged across all replicas via AllReduce every T steps. Building on this ensemble sub- strate, we further propose an automatic learning rate (auto-LR) controller that treats the relative training loss across replicas as a performance signal, updating the shared base schedule toward higher-performing configurations via a momentum- based gradient-free meta-update. The combined method produces a self-adapting learning rate schedule that improves both optimization quality and generalization without additional hyperparameter sweeps or training budget. Crucially, the framework generalizes beyond learning rate: any scalar hyperparam- eter that does not alter model architecture—such as dropout rate, attention scale temperature, or weight-decay coefficient—can be explored across replicas using the same fan-out/converge protocol, with inter-replica loss differences serving as zero-order hypergradients that guide the search direction. HDET is imple- mented as a drop-in replacement for PyTorch’s OneCycleLR scheduler, requiring no changes to model architecture, optimizer, or data pipeline. Code is available at https://github.com/hailingc/ensemble_training.
